source_text: Nam cum inauditum monstrum sit, si dogma etiam tolerabile, novum tamen, aliquis relin quens propria abusivis verbis condere ambiguisque conetur, tum istud infinite deformius est, quod res obscaenas et Dei iustitiam criminantes tam ancipitibus Augustinus nititur confirmare sententiis, ut eas contra se proprie, pro se autem precario sonare fateatur. Quisquamne eruditorum illi argumento fidat, quod, cum in ius venerit, ab inimico eius quasi vernaculum, ab illo vero quasi fugitivum plagiatumque pensetur?
pass_a_gloss: For when it is an unheard monster if someone, even a tolerable dogma, yet new, leaving proper things tries to found it by abusive and ambiguous words, then that is infinitely more deformed, that Augustine strives to confirm obscene things accusing the justice of God by sentences so two-edged that he confesses they sound properly against him, but for him precariously. Would any of the learned trust that argument which, when it has come into court, is weighed by his enemy as house-born, but by him as runaway and kidnapped?
pass_b_english: It would be an unheard-of monstrosity if someone tried to establish even a tolerable but novel doctrine by abandoning exact expressions for inexact and ambiguous ones. How infinitely more disgraceful, then, that Augustine tries to establish obscene claims accusing God’s justice through statements so double-edged that he admits they speak properly against him and only by indulgence in his favor! What educated person would trust an argument that, once it came to court, his opponent could claim as a slave born in his household, while he himself could possess it only as a runaway he had kidnapped?

choices.why: Julian's forensic virtue that renders to each his own, without fraude or gratia (partiality).
rejected: righteousness (Pauline overlay unless the verse forces it)

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
